title: Password reset links fail once, then work a few seconds later
scenario: About 4% of password reset attempts return invalid_token on the first click, but succeed if the user clicks again 5 to 10 seconds later. The reset token is written to the primary database, while validation reads from a read replica. During evening traffic the replica lag is normally 2 seconds and sometimes spikes to 12 seconds.
goal: Find the cause of the first-click failures and choose a production-safe fix that makes password reset validation correct.

concepts.name: Password reset token
concepts.summary: A temporary secret link value that proves the user controls the email account. It is usually short-lived and should be treated as security-sensitive.
concepts.used_here: The token is created during the reset request and later checked when the user clicks the email link.

concepts.name: Primary database
concepts.summary: The database node that accepts writes and is the source of truth. Reads from it see committed writes immediately, subject to transaction isolation.
concepts.used_here: Password reset tokens are written to the primary database.

concepts.name: Read replica
concepts.summary: A database copy used to serve read traffic. It receives changes from the primary after they commit, often asynchronously.
concepts.used_here: The validation path reads reset tokens from a replica instead of the primary.

concepts.name: Replication lag
concepts.summary: The delay between a write committing on the primary and becoming visible on a replica. With asynchronous replication, this delay can vary under load.
concepts.used_here: Evening lag is usually 2 seconds but can spike to 12 seconds, which can hide newly created tokens from validation reads.

concepts.name: Application logs
concepts.summary: Records emitted by services while handling requests. Good logs include timestamps, request IDs, database host names, and important decision outcomes.
concepts.used_here: Logs can show when a token was created, which database handled validation, and why validation returned invalid_token.

concepts.name: Monitoring metrics
concepts.summary: Numeric time-series used to understand system behavior over time. Examples include error rate, latency, query rate, and replication lag.
concepts.used_here: Metrics help correlate invalid_token responses with replica lag and later confirm the fix.

concepts.name: Token TTL
concepts.summary: A time-to-live is how long a token remains valid before it expires. It controls lifetime, not whether a newly written row is visible on a replica.
concepts.used_here: Increasing the TTL would not make a just-created token appear sooner on the read replica.

concepts.name: Rate limiting
concepts.summary: A control that blocks or slows requests when a user or IP sends too many. It protects services from abuse and overload.
concepts.used_here: It is a plausible cause of auth failures, but the symptom is invalid_token followed by success seconds later.

concepts.name: Single-use token
concepts.summary: A token that is consumed after one successful use. This prevents a reset link from being reused after it has changed the password.
concepts.used_here: A consumed token would normally fail on the second click, not fail first and then succeed.

concepts.name: Read-your-writes consistency
concepts.summary: A guarantee that after a client writes data, later reads by that client see that write. Systems with replicas often need explicit routing or waiting to provide it.
concepts.used_here: Password reset validation needs to see the token that was just created for the user.

concepts.name: Log sequence number
concepts.summary: A log sequence number is a database position that identifies how far a node has applied writes. A replica at or beyond a given position has applied that write.
concepts.used_here: The service can record the write position for the token and only read from a replica that has caught up to it.

concepts.name: Primary read load
concepts.summary: Read traffic sent to the primary database instead of replicas. It improves freshness but uses capacity on the write node.
concepts.used_here: Validating reset tokens on the primary increases primary reads, so capacity and latency must be watched.

concepts.name: Feature flag
concepts.summary: A runtime switch that enables a behavior for some or all traffic without redeploying code. It allows gradual rollout and quick rollback.
concepts.used_here: The fix can be enabled for a small percentage of reset validations before full rollout.

concepts.name: Latency
concepts.summary: The time a request takes to complete. Higher database load can increase latency even if requests still succeed.
concepts.used_here: The rollout must check that primary validation does not make reset or login requests too slow.

steps.title: Start with the most useful evidence
steps.question: You are on call and can inspect logs and dashboards. What should you check first to distinguish a visibility problem from a token-generation problem?

options.text: Sample token strings from failed requests and look for collisions or malformed token values in the generator.
options.hint: A generator issue would usually affect the same token consistently. Here the same user action starts working shortly afterward.

options.text: Compare token creation time, validation time, database host used for validation, and replica lag for failed and successful clicks.
Check whether the token TTL was lowered during evening traffic and whether users are clicking after expiration.
options.hint: The users succeed 5 to 10 seconds later with the same reset flow. That pattern is not what you expect from a token that has already expired.

options.text: Review rate-limit decisions for the affected IPs and verify whether the reset endpoint is blocking repeated clicks.
options.hint: Rate limits usually make repeated attempts worse, not better. Focus on what changes between the first click and the second click a few seconds later.

steps.explanation: The key question is whether validation is reading a database view that includes the freshly written token. Correlating creation time, validation database host, and replica lag can explain why a first click fails while a second click 5 to 10 seconds later succeeds. TTL and rate limiting are tempting checks, but they do not match a failure that heals after waiting a few seconds.

steps.title: Interpret the request trace
steps.question: The trace for one affected user shows: token created on the primary at 20:14:03, first validation read from replica-a at 20:14:04 returned no row, replica-a lag was 9 seconds, second validation from replica-a at 20:14:11 found the row. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The token was consumed by the first click, and the second click succeeded because the consume operation retried later.
options.hint: A single-use token becomes less available after a successful consume, not more available after a failed lookup. The first read returned no row, so it did not consume the token.

options.text: The reset token expired before the first click because the TTL was too short for evening traffic.
options.hint: The first click happened 1 second after creation, and the second click at 8 seconds found the token. Expiration would not normally reverse itself.

options.text: The first validation read from an asynchronously replicated replica before the token write had reached it.
The primary database rolled back the token write and then recreated the token during the second click.
options.hint: The trace says the token was created once on the primary at 20:14:03. The changing fact is whether the replica had applied that write.

steps.explanation: At 20:14:04 the replica was 9 seconds behind, so it could only see primary writes from roughly 20:13:55 or earlier. The token written at 20:14:03 was not visible yet, so validation incorrectly returned invalid_token. TTL is the most tempting alternative, but the token was only 1 second old on the failed click and was valid on the later click.

steps.title: Choose the immediate corrective change
steps.question: You need a fix that stops incorrect invalid_token responses for newly created password reset links. Which change is the best immediate production fix?

options.text: Restart the lagging replica during evening traffic whenever invalid_token crosses 1%.
options.hint: The incident happens during normal asynchronous lag spikes, not necessarily a broken process. Restarting can also increase lag while the replica catches up.

options.text: Validate password reset tokens by reading from the primary database instead of the read replica.
Increase the reset token TTL from 15 minutes to 60 minutes so tokens remain valid through replica lag spikes.
options.hint: The token is not expiring; it is temporarily invisible to the reader. A longer lifetime does not make a replica apply a fresh write sooner.

options.text: Keep validation on the replica, but retry once after 2 seconds when validation returns invalid_token.
options.hint: The lag sometimes spikes to 12 seconds. A fixed 2-second retry still returns false negatives during the exact condition causing the incident.

steps.explanation: Reading from the primary gives validation a current view of the token row after the creation transaction commits. This directly fixes a visibility problem and is appropriate for a security-sensitive, user-facing flow. Increasing TTL is tempting because the symptom says invalid_token, but the failing token is only seconds old while lag can be as high as 12 seconds.

steps.title: Reduce load without losing correctness
steps.question: After routing all reset validation reads to the primary, the incident stops, but primary read load rises during evening traffic. Which design can reduce primary reads while still guaranteeing that validation sees the token write?

options.text: Record the primary commit position for the token and read from a replica only after it has reached that position, otherwise use the primary.
Delay sending every reset email by 5 seconds so most replicas have time to catch up.
options.hint: A 5-second delay cannot guarantee correctness when lag sometimes reaches 12 seconds. It also adds user-visible delay to every reset request.

options.text: Keep each user sticky to one replica for 10 minutes after they request a password reset.
options.hint: Stickiness helps when a user wrote to the same node they later read from. Here the write went to the primary, and the sticky replica can still be behind.

options.text: Send validation to the replica with the lowest average lag over the last minute.
options.hint: Average lag does not prove a specific token write has arrived. A replica can look healthy on average and still be behind the write you need.

steps.explanation: A commit position lets the service make a precise freshness check: the replica is safe only if it has applied the token write. If no replica has caught up, falling back to the primary preserves correctness. Choosing the lowest-lag replica is tempting, but low average lag is not the same as proving that this specific write is visible.

steps.title: Roll out the fix safely
steps.question: You are ready to deploy primary-or-caught-up-replica validation. What rollout plan is safest?

options.text: Raise the invalid_token alert threshold from 1% to 5% during rollout to avoid noisy pages.
options.hint: The current incident is about a 4% failure rate, so hiding that signal would make validation harder. Rollout needs more visibility, not less.

options.text: Enable it for 100% of traffic immediately because the logic is correct and the old path is known bad.
options.hint: Correct logic can still create capacity or latency problems. A safe rollout should limit blast radius and keep a fast rollback path.

options.text: Use a feature flag to ramp from 5% to 25% to 100%, while watching invalid_token rate, primary read QPS, and reset latency.
Enable it only for users who fail once, so primary load increases only after invalid_token has already happened.
options.hint: That reduces load, but it preserves the bad first-click experience. The goal is to prevent the false invalid_token, not recover after it.

steps.explanation: A staged feature-flag rollout proves both correctness and capacity before all users depend on the new path. The important metrics are the user-visible failure rate plus the primary load and latency introduced by fresher reads. Enabling for only users who already failed is tempting for load control, but it still makes users hit the first-click bug.

steps.title: Confirm the incident is fixed
steps.question: After the rollout reaches 100%, which observation best confirms the fix worked without creating a new database problem?

options.text: The number of password reset requests per evening stays the same, and no users report expired links after 15 minutes.
options.hint: Request volume and expiration reports do not directly measure the original false invalid_token problem. You need to look at first-click validation outcomes.

options.text: Replica lag drops from 12 seconds to under 2 seconds, and reset email volume remains unchanged.
options.hint: The fix changes where validation reads from; it does not make replication itself faster. Replica lag may remain variable even when the user flow is fixed.

options.text: First-click invalid_token for newly created reset links falls from 4% to near baseline, second-click recovery clusters disappear, and primary read latency stays within limits.
All validation reads move to replicas again after the evening peak, and primary read QPS returns to its old value.
options.hint: Returning to the old read path can reintroduce the stale-read failure. Lower primary QPS is only good if the consistency guarantee remains in place.

steps.explanation: The original symptom was a 4% first-click invalid_token rate followed by success 5 to 10 seconds later, so those patterns should disappear. The fix may leave replica lag unchanged, because it avoids stale reads rather than speeding replication. You also need primary read latency and load to remain healthy so the correctness fix does not create a capacity incident.

takeaway: When a flow writes to a primary and immediately reads from a replica, asynchronous replication can produce false negatives. For security-sensitive freshly created tokens, use the primary or an explicit read-your-writes mechanism such as waiting for a replica to reach the write position. Increasing TTL treats expiration, not visibility, and will not fix stale reads.
